question: Which of the following is NOT correctly matched? [Voyage Milestone — Location / Geographical Feature reached]
options: Vasco da Gama (1498) — Anchored at Kappad near Calicut on the Malabar Coast of India
Bartolomeu Dias (1488) — Discovered and rounded the Cape of Good Hope, reaching the Great Fish River
Pêro da Covilhã (1487–1489) — Travelled overland via Cairo and Aden to Malabar (India) to scout trade ports
Vasco da Gama (1497) — Discovered Brazil while executing a wide sweep (volta do mar) in the South Atlantic
wrong_fact: Vasco da Gama did NOT discover Brazil on his 1497 voyage. It was Pedro Álvares Cabral who made a wide sweep (volta do mar) and accidentally sighted and landed on the coast of Brazil in April 1500, during the second Portuguese expedition to India.
explanation: While Vasco da Gama did perform a wide swing into the South Atlantic to catch favorable winds (known as the 'volta do mar' or 'great loop'), he did not reach or discover Brazil. It was his successor Pedro Álvares Cabral who swung even wider in 1500 and landed on the Brazilian coast before continuing to India. The other options are correct: Gama anchored at Kappad (Calicut) in 1498; Dias rounded the Cape in 1488; Pêro da Covilhã successfully completed a secret overland mission to spy on the spice ports of India.

question: Which of the following is NOT correctly matched? [Explorer / Envoy — Route details and Indian Ocean Pilot]
options: Vasco da Gama — Guided from Malindi (East Africa) to Calicut (India) by a legendary pilot, often identified as Kanji Malam or Ahmad ibn Mājid
Afonso de Paiva — Travelled overland with Pêro da Covilhã to find the Christian kingdom of Prester John in Ethiopia but died in Cairo
Diogo Cão — Discovered the mouth of the Congo River and sailed as far south as Cape Cross (Namibia) in the 1480s
Bartholomeu Dias — Guided from the Cape of Good Hope to the coast of Cochin by the famous Arab navigator Ahmad ibn Mājid
wrong_fact: Bartholomeu Dias did NOT sail to the coast of Cochin, nor was he guided by Ahmad ibn Mājid. Dias's crew mutinied near the Great Fish River on the southeast coast of Africa, forcing him to turn back to Portugal in 1488 without ever crossing the Indian Ocean to India.
explanation: Bartholomeu Dias only reached the eastern edge of South Africa (Kwaaihoek/Great Fish River) and never crossed the Indian Ocean. It was Vasco da Gama who, ten years later, engaged a pilot (often identified as Ahmad ibn Mājid or Kanji Malam) at Malindi to cross the Indian Ocean to Calicut. Diogo Cão successfully charted the West African coast to Namibia, and Afonso de Paiva died in Cairo before reaching Ethiopia.

question: Which of the following is NOT correctly matched? [Ocean Current / Maritime Zone — Crucial role in the Portuguese search for a sea route to India]
options: Volta do Mar ('Turn of the Sea') — Sailing strategy of heading far west/southwest into the open Atlantic to bypass the contrary currents and winds of the West African coast
Benguela Current — A warm, southward-flowing current along the East African coast that Vasco da Gama struggled to sail against near Mozambique
Southwest Monsoon Winds — Strong seasonal winds blowing from Africa toward India between June and September; Vasco da Gama used them to cross the Arabian Sea to Calicut
Northeast Monsoon Winds — Seasonal winds blowing from India toward Africa between October and February; Vasco da Gama utilized them on his return voyage to Africa
wrong_fact: The Benguela Current is a COLD, NORTHWARD-flowing current located along the WEST (Atlantic) coast of Southern Africa (Namibia/South Africa). It is not a warm, southward current, nor is it located along the East African coast. The current along the East African coast that flows southward is the warm Agulhas/Mozambique Current.
explanation: The Benguela Current flows along the west coast of Africa in a northerly direction, bringing cold water from the Southern Ocean. Explorers heading south had to sail far out into the Atlantic (volta do mar) to avoid sailing directly against this current and the prevailing southeasterly winds. The other details are correct: the monsoon winds (Southwest for going to India, Northeast for returning) were critical for crossing the Arabian Sea, and the Volta do Mar was the standard Atlantic route strategy.
